logo_override.validation_detail: png 512x512, probed via webfetch -> 'Image fetched successfully' (HTTP 200 + image content type); the Foundation's own crest - the black 'G' enclosing Calouste Sarkis Gulbenkian's quadriga - near-black on an opaque white rounded square, so it stays legible on a light card
logo_override._award: Gulbenkian Institute for Advanced Study Fellowships 2027/28

notes:
Awarding body is Fundacao Calouste Gulbenkian, so the Foundation's own mark is correct. Rule 3 drove this result. The site header logo, https://gulbenkian.pt/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/01_logotipo_web_fundacao_EN_50px.svg (alt 'Fundacao Calouste Gulbenkian', in
), probed 200 but I read the SVG source and EVERY path is style="fill:#fff" on a transparent field - the exact white-on-transparent failure rule 3 forbids, since the site only ever draws it on the black header. I then hunted for a dark variant as rule 3 directs: enumerated every image the page references (only that one logo, the favicon set, article thumbnails and two footer certification marks ISO-14001_preto.svg / livro_reclamacoes_preto-01.svg, which are not the Foundation's logo); read the theme stylesheet /wp-content/themes/fcg-common/dist/assets/style-B05ln7Nj.css and it contains no url(...) logo reference at all, because the logo is a plain in markup; and the WordPress media REST API (/wp-json/wp/v2/media?search=logotipo) is closed to anonymous callers with HTTP 401. So no dark wordmark is published on gulbenkian.pt. Falling back to the favicon family, which the brief allows as a last resort: the site's own manifest.webmanifest names icon-192x192.png and icon-512x512.png, and these are not generic browser icons but the Foundation's crest itself. I probed both icon-512x512.png (chosen, highest resolution) and apple-icon-180x180.png - both returned 200 with an image content type. Note the asset sits under the theme's .../favicon/ directory, but it is the identical artwork that the white wordmark wraps around the text of, so it is the body's mark and not a browser glyph.
